rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window and reduce the chance of missing late compounds. This run should show whether peaks are compressed early, late, or across the gradient so the next injections can trim phi and adjust slope intelligently.

All 10 compounds eluted well within the gradient, so trim the solvent window to the actual elution region to improve efficiency and likely cut time without sacrificing full elution. This keeps the gradient focused around the observed peak window and tests whether the critical mid-cluster gains or loses resolution under a narrower phi range.

The broad window was clearly better; now test a steeper version to reduce runtime while checking whether the critical 6/7 pair is slope-sensitive. Comparing this directly to injection 1 isolates the effect of gradient steepness on the clustered middle peaks.

The steeper 10 min gradient won on time but over-compressed the central cluster, so move to an intermediate slope between injections 1 and 3. This directly probes whether the 5–7 region regains enough resolution while keeping runtime short enough to preserve a high CRF.

The only remaining issue is the 6/7 pair, and resolution improved strongly as tG increased from 10 to 14 min, so a slightly shallower 16 min gradient is the logical next refinement. It should improve that pair further while likely staying short enough to keep the time penalty negligible.

Since the 6/7 pair responds to slope but the best CRF is still at 14 min, temperature is now the best lever to test for a selectivity gain without adding runtime penalty. A 5 C decrease may slightly spread or reorder the critical central pair while keeping all compounds comfortably within the run.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity in the critical cluster, so test the opposite direction to see whether a modest increase improves the 6/7 separation at the same near-optimal slope. This isolates temperature selectivity around the current best method without introducing a time penalty.

Temperature did not improve selectivity, so return to 40 C and continue the clearer trend that a shallower gradient resolves the critical pair. An 18 min gradient tests whether resolution gains can outweigh the modest added time penalty better than the 16 min run.

The best region is clearly around 14 min at 40 C, and all peaks elute by ~9.4 min, so slightly lowering phi1 may redistribute the central cluster without lengthening the run much. This probes whether a modestly narrower high-end window can improve the stubborn 6/7 selectivity while staying near the current optimum.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved CRF while preserving a zero time penalty, so continue in the same direction with a slightly narrower gradient window. This may further reshape the central cluster and improve the limiting 6/7 pair without pushing runtime beyond the penalty threshold.

With phi1 = 0.90 giving the best CRF, test a slightly steeper gradient to see if the run can be shortened further while keeping the critical pair near acceptable resolution. This explores whether the zero-penalty region extends to shorter tG at the improved phi window.

At phi1 = 0.90, shortening to 12 min over-compressed the critical pair, so test the opposite direction and see whether a slightly shallower gradient can raise the resolution term to 1.000. If the added runtime remains below the time-penalty threshold, this could surpass the current best.

The best method is likely near phi1 = 0.90 and tG = 14, so now probe phi0 since the first peak is still quite early and the low-end window may be wider than needed. Raising phi0 slightly could rebalance the gradient and subtly improve selectivity in the crowded middle without materially affecting runtime.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved the best CRF, so continue that trend with a small additional increase while keeping the successful phi1 and tG fixed. This tests whether further trimming the low-end window sharpens selectivity in the central cluster without causing the first peak to become effectively unretained.

The best result came from phi0 = 0.10 and phi1 = 0.90, while lowering phi1 helped at phi0 = 0.05, so combine those favorable changes. This tests whether a slightly narrower overall window around the successful low-end trim can push the resolution term to 1.000 without incurring a time penalty.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so this run is a local robustness check around the optimum by trimming phi0 one more step while keeping the other successful settings fixed. It may reveal an equally optimal, slightly faster alternative or confirm that the current best method sits at the top of the plateau.

The optimum appears to sit near phi0 = 0.10 with a narrowed upper window, so reduce phi1 one more step from the winning method to probe the local boundary of the optimum plateau. This could retain full resolution while slightly concentrating the useful gradient range, but if it starts adding time penalty we will know injection 15 is truly best.

Since phi0 = 0.10 and phi1 = 0.85 is optimal, the remaining unexplored adjacent point is a small increase in phi0 at the same successful upper limit. This checks whether the optimum is centered exactly at 0.10 or whether a similarly perfect plateau extends to 0.15.

Now that two methods have reached the maximum CRF at 40 C, use remaining injections to map robustness around that optimum plateau. Testing the winning solvent window at 45 C checks whether temperature tolerance exists or whether 40 C is uniquely required for full score.

Since 45 C strongly worsened the critical pair at an otherwise optimal solvent program, test 35 C on the alternate 1.000-scoring method to complete the temperature robustness picture. This confirms whether the optimum plateau is centered specifically at 40 C or if one solvent window tolerates lower temperature better.

With 40 C established as the temperature optimum, use the remaining runs to map the high-scoring solvent plateau around the second 1.000 method. Lowering phi1 one step from 0.85 on the phi0 = 0.15 branch tests the local edge of that optimum region.

The optimum at 40 C appears narrow in temperature, but the critical pair switches behavior at lower temperature; combining 35 C with a steeper gradient may counterbalance that extra retention and reveal a different selectivity-time tradeoff. With the maximum already achieved, this is a worthwhile exploratory run for an alternate operating point near the best solvent window.

One remaining question is whether stronger slope compensation can rescue the poor high-temperature selectivity at the otherwise optimal solvent window. This run tests the orthogonality of temperature and gradient steepness around the best method while avoiding duplication of any prior setting.

For the final two runs, stay near the 1.000-scoring plateau and test whether the phi0 = 0.15 branch can tolerate a slightly steeper gradient without losing too much resolution. This helps define the fastest near-optimal method adjacent to the current maxima.

For the final run, probe the remaining adjacent corner of the 40 C high-performing region by combining the higher phi0 branch with the lower phi1 branch. This completes the local map around the 1.000 plateau and tests whether a more aggressively trimmed window can still maintain full resolution without time penalty.
